Wait — for a product page, rendering calls: getRecommendations (recommendationservice) and chooseAd (adservice) — both async? In the template, `ad` and `recommendations` are computed before rendering in productHandler? Let's recall v0.10.3 productHandler:

```go
func (fe *frontendServer) productHandler(...) {
	id := mux.Vars(r)["id"]
	...
	log.WithField("id", id).WithField("currency", currentCurrency(r)).Debug("serving product page")
	p, err := fe.getProduct(r.Context(), id)
	currencies, err := fe.getCurrencies(r.Context())
	cart, err := fe.getCart(r.Context(), sessionID(r))
	price, err := fe.convertCurrency(...)
	recommendations, err := fe.getRecommendations(r.Context(), sessionID(r), []string{id})
	...
	product := struct{...}{..., Recommendations: recommendations, ...}
	// then executeTemplate with "ad": fe.chooseAd(...)
```
Hmm, the order: in v0.10.3 the product handler logs "serving product page" right at the beginning (before fetching), as we see (log line immediately after start). Then it does: getProduct, getCurrencies, getCart, convertCurrency, getRecommendations, then render (which calls chooseAd).

So the stall after "serving product page" is in getProduct/getCurrencies/getCart/convert/recommendations/render+ads.

Both requests unblocked at the same instant, 1.5µs apart. Note: they both began at ~19.166 and ~19.238, and both finished at 19.388. 

The difference: 221 - 150 = 71ms = the difference in start times (19.2378 - 19.1664 = 71.4ms). Exactly! So both requests were blocked from their respective start until the same moment 19.388. This means: from the very beginning of their handling (right after the near-instant "serving product page" log), both were blocked on something that was released at 19.38807.

That means the blocking started at/just after the start of each request. So the shared blocker was already stalled when they arrived, and released at 19.388.

The first thing after "serving product page"... the calls are getProduct (catalog), getCurrencies (currency), getCart (cart), getRecommendations (recommendation → catalog). If one downstream service was stalled, all requests calling it would stall.

But two different connections? Both product pages would call the same set. If the stalled one is catalog or currency or cart or recommendation, both would block on it. Their resumption at the same instant indicates that service answered both at the same instant — i.e., the stalled service resumed and processed both queued requests.

Hmm, but if the stalled service resumed and processed two requests, the responses wouldn't be exactly 1.5µs apart... well, plausible: a Node.js/Python service processing two queued requests back-to-back takes ~1ms each. Hmm, 1.5µs is too tight for two separate gRPC round trips. Unless both responses arrived in the same TCP segment (HTTP/2 multiplexing) — very likely! If both frontend streams are on the SAME gRPC connection (e.g. to currencyservice), and the service replied to both, the responses could be delivered in the same flush/segment → both goroutines unblock within µs.

So: a single gRPC connection stalled for ~200ms then delivered multiple responses at once. This strongly suggests a *network-level stall* on one connection (packet loss with RTO ~200ms, or a stalled receiver).

So the picture: ~200ms stalls on individual frontend↔downstream connections, each stall affecting all streams on that connection.

This is decisive: the stalls are NOT specific to one downstream service or to the frontend. checkoutservice's calls to emailservice and paymentservice stall ~200-210ms occasionally, while its other steps are 2-9ms.

So: intermittent ~200ms stalls across many different service-to-service calls: frontend→cart, frontend→currency/catalog/ads (indirect), checkout→email, checkout→payment. Different pods, different callee. Common factor: the node / the CNI / cluster network path.

This strongly supports: a cluster/node-level network fault causing packet loss (TCP retransmission ~200ms). All pods are on ONE node (tiktok-k8s-lab-control-plane). So a node-level network problem (e.g., packet loss on the node's networking: veth/bridge/CNI, or the node's NIC, or a netem/qdisc rule applied at the node level, or conntrack pressure) would intermittently delay any TCP flow.

And the ~200ms quantum = Linux TCP RTO_MIN, consistent with a single lost packet + retransmission per event. Also observed ~372, ~531, ~660 samples = multiple retransmissions (RTO backoff 200/400...).

Also consistent with the "simultaneous release" pair: two requests on the same connection (or two connections whose lost packets were retransmitted at the same moment) unblock together. Hmm, for the pair at 19.388, if both connections lost a packet at ~19.17-19.19, they'd retransmit at 19.37-19.39 → plausibly simultaneously (both ~200ms after their respective losses, and their losses could coincide within the same drop burst).

So the root cause: intermittent packet loss/delay in the node's pod network path, causing TCP retransmissions (~200ms RTO) on many service-to-service calls; no errors because TCP retransmits recover.

Now — can I distinguish "packet loss" from "one-way latency spike"? The signature at exactly ~200ms (RTO_MIN) points to loss+retransmit, not delay.
